subject: ela
intro: When you listen to a speaker, you can break their argument into parts. The argument is the overall position the speaker wants you to accept. A claim is a single statement the speaker wants you to believe. A reason tells why a claim is true, and evidence is the concrete proof, such as a fact, an example, or a number. In each problem, read the speaker's words as if you were hearing them, then answer the question about the spoken argument.

items.prompt:
Read this transcript of a student speaking at a class meeting, then answer the question.

"Good morning. I think our class should start a recycling program. Right now we throw away a lot of paper that could be reused. Last week our class custodian told me that our room fills two large trash bags with paper every single day. If we put a recycling bin in the corner, that paper could be recycled instead of thrown away. A recycling program would help our school and teach us a good habit. Please vote yes for a recycling bin. Thank you."

What is the speaker's overall argument?
items.answer: The speaker argues that the class should start a recycling program by adding a recycling bin.

steps: The overall argument is the position the speaker wants the audience to accept, not just the topic.
The speaker opens by saying, "I think our class should start a recycling program," and ends by asking the class to "vote yes for a recycling bin."
These statements show the position the speaker is trying to get the audience to support.
So the speaker's overall argument is that the class should start a recycling program by adding a recycling bin.

items.prompt:
Read this transcript of a student giving an announcement, then answer the question.

"Hi everyone. I am here to tell you that the school library should stay open after school. Many students need a quiet place to do homework. In a survey our class did last month, forty out of sixty students said they have no quiet place to study at home. If the library stayed open one extra hour, those students would have somewhere to work. Keeping the library open would help us all do better in school. Please support this idea."

What is one piece of evidence the speaker uses to support the argument?
items.answer: In a survey, forty out of sixty students said they have no quiet place to study at home.

steps: Evidence is concrete proof such as a fact, an example, or a number the speaker gives.
The speaker states, "In a survey our class did last month, forty out of sixty students said they have no quiet place to study at home."
This is a specific number from a survey, so it is evidence, not just an opinion.
The piece of evidence is that forty out of sixty students said they have no quiet place to study at home.

items.prompt:
Read this transcript of a student speaking to the class, then answer the question.

"Good afternoon. I believe our school should add a soccer team. A lot of students love soccer and would join. When I asked around the cafeteria, twenty-five students said they would sign up for a soccer team if we had one. A team would give them a fun way to stay active and make friends. Other nearby schools already have soccer teams, so we should too. Please tell the principal you support a school soccer team."

What is the main claim the speaker wants the audience to accept?
items.answer: The school should add a soccer team.

steps: A claim is a statement the speaker wants the listener to accept.
The speaker says, "I believe our school should add a soccer team," and ends by asking listeners to support a school soccer team.
The other lines, such as the number of students who would sign up, are support for that claim, not the claim itself.
So the main claim is that the school should add a soccer team.

items.prompt:
Read this transcript of a student speaking at lunch, then answer the question.

"Hey everyone. We need a longer lunch period. Right now lunch is only twenty minutes, and many of us cannot finish eating in time. The cafeteria line alone takes about ten minutes, which leaves only ten minutes to eat. A longer lunch would let us eat without rushing. It would also give us a short break in a long day. Please ask the office for a thirty-minute lunch."

Which statement from the speech is a piece of evidence rather than a claim?
items.answer: The cafeteria line alone takes about ten minutes.

steps: Evidence is a concrete fact or number the speaker offers as proof.
The claim is the position the speaker wants accepted: "We need a longer lunch period."
The line "The cafeteria line alone takes about ten minutes" gives a specific number that supports the claim.
A number used as proof is evidence, so this statement is evidence rather than a claim.

items.prompt:
Read this transcript of a student speaking at a club meeting, then answer the question.

"Good morning, club members. Our art club should meet twice a week instead of once. We have many projects to finish and not enough time. Last month we had to leave three paintings unfinished because we ran out of meeting days. Meeting twice a week would give us time to complete our work. I hope you will vote for two meetings a week. Thank you."

What reason does the speaker give for why the club should meet twice a week?
items.answer: The club has many projects to finish and not enough time to complete them.

steps: A reason tells why a claim is true.
The claim is that the art club should meet twice a week.
The speaker explains, "We have many projects to finish and not enough time," which tells why the claim is true.
So the reason is that the club has many projects to finish and not enough time to complete them.

items.prompt:
Read this transcript of a student speaking to the class, then answer the question.

"Hello, classmates. I think we should have a class pet, like a small fish. A fish is easy to care for and does not make noise. Taking turns feeding it would teach us responsibility. A fish tank would also make our room feel calmer and more welcoming. Caring for a pet would be a great experience for everyone. Please raise your hand if you would like a class fish."

Does the speaker support the claim that a fish is easy to care for with a clear reason, or is it left without support? Explain what the speaker said.
items.answer: It is left without support. The speaker states that a fish is easy to care for but gives no reason or evidence to prove it.

steps: A claim is supported when the speaker gives a reason or evidence; it is unsupported when the speaker only states it.
The speaker says, "A fish is easy to care for and does not make noise," but never explains why a fish is easy to care for.
No fact, example, or reason is given to back up that the fish is easy to care for.
So the claim is left without support; the speaker simply states it.

items.prompt:
Read this transcript of a student giving a short speech, then answer the question.

"Good afternoon. Our class should plant a small garden in the courtyard. A garden would give us fresh vegetables to share. It would also be a place to learn about how plants grow. Mr. Lopez, our science teacher, said he would help us pick seeds and tools. With his help, the garden could be ready by spring. Please support our class garden. Thank you for listening."

What is the topic the speaker is talking about?
items.answer: Planting a small garden in the school courtyard.

steps: The topic is the subject the speech is about, not the speaker's position.
Throughout the speech, the speaker talks about planting a garden in the courtyard.
The topic is what the whole speech focuses on.
So the topic is planting a small garden in the school courtyard.

items.prompt:

"Hi everyone. I think our school should sell water bottles in the cafeteria. Many students get thirsty during the day and have nothing to drink. The water fountain near the gym has been broken for two weeks, so students cannot refill bottles there. Selling water bottles would make sure no one goes without water. Please ask the office to add water bottles to the lunch line."

Which claim is the speaker trying to prove?
items.answer: The school should sell water bottles in the cafeteria.

steps: A claim is the statement the speaker wants the audience to accept.
The speaker says, "I think our school should sell water bottles in the cafeteria," and asks the office to add them to the lunch line.
The broken fountain is a fact used to support that claim, not the claim itself.
So the claim the speaker is trying to prove is that the school should sell water bottles in the cafeteria.

"Good morning. We should start a book swap shelf in our classroom. Many of us have books at home that we have already finished reading. A shelf in our room could do the same. Please help me set one up."

What piece of evidence does the speaker give to support the book swap idea?
items.answer: Last year, the class next door tried a book swap and traded over one hundred books in a month.

steps: Evidence is concrete proof, such as an example or a number.
The speaker says, "Last year, the class next door tried a book swap and traded over one hundred books in a month."

items.prompt:
Read this transcript of a student speaking at a club meeting, then answer the question.

"Hello, everyone. Our chess club should buy three new chess sets. We have grown to fifteen members, but we only own four chess boards. That means many members have to wait their turn instead of playing. With three more sets, almost everyone could play at the same time. Please vote to buy the new chess sets so no one has to sit out."

What reason does the speaker give for buying three new chess sets?
items.answer: The club has fifteen members but only four boards, so many members have to wait instead of playing.

steps: A reason explains why the claim is true.
The claim is that the chess club should buy three new chess sets.
The speaker explains, "We have grown to fifteen members, but we only own four chess boards," so members have to wait their turn.
So the reason is that there are too few boards for the number of members, forcing some to wait.

items.prompt:

"Good afternoon. I believe our school should hold a spring talent show. A talent show would let students share their skills, like singing, dancing, and juggling. It would also be a fun event for families to attend. Last spring, the school across town held a talent show, and more than two hundred people came to watch. Our school could host a great show too. Please tell your teacher you support a spring talent show."

What is the speaker's overall argument?
items.answer: The speaker argues that the school should hold a spring talent show.

steps: The overall argument is the position the speaker wants the audience to accept.
The speaker opens with, "I believe our school should hold a spring talent show," and ends by asking listeners to support it.
The talent and the number of attendees are support, not the argument itself.

items.prompt:
Read this transcript of a student speaking to the class, then answer the question.

"Hi everyone. I think our class should take a field trip to the science museum. The museum is the most amazing place in the whole world, and it is just the best. Everyone would love it so much. A trip there would be incredible and unforgettable. Please ask our teacher to plan a trip to the science museum."

Does the speaker support the claim that the class should visit the science museum with evidence, or is it left unsupported? Explain.
items.answer: It is left unsupported. The speaker only uses strong opinion words like amazing, best, and incredible, but gives no facts or reasons.

steps: A claim is supported when the speaker gives reasons or evidence, not just strong feelings.
The speaker calls the museum "the most amazing place in the whole world" and "the best," which are opinions.
No fact, example, or reason is given to show why the class should go.
Because the speaker offers only opinion and excited words, the claim is left unsupported.

items.prompt:
Read this transcript of a student speaking at a meeting, then answer the question.

"Good morning. Our class should keep the lights off near the windows on sunny days. When the sun is bright, the room is already lit well enough without the lights. Turning off those lights would save electricity and lower the school's costs. Our custodian said the school pays a high bill for lighting each month. Please remember to switch off the window-side lights on sunny days."

Which statement from the speech is a claim the speaker wants the audience to accept?
items.answer: Our class should keep the lights off near the windows on sunny days.

steps: A claim is a statement the speaker wants the listener to accept and act on.
The speaker says, "Our class should keep the lights off near the windows on sunny days," and repeats the request at the end.
The fact that the room is already lit and that the school pays a high bill are support for that claim.
So the claim the speaker wants accepted is that the class should keep the window-side lights off on sunny days.

items.prompt:
Read this transcript of a student speaking at a club meeting, then answer the question.

"Good afternoon. Our garden club should meet in the morning instead of after school. Many members have sports practice in the afternoon and cannot come. Last week, only three of our twelve members showed up to the afternoon meeting. A morning meeting would let more members join. Please vote to switch our meetings to the morning."

What piece of evidence does the speaker give to support meeting in the morning?
items.answer: Last week, only three of the club's twelve members showed up to the afternoon meeting.

steps: Evidence is a concrete fact or number used as proof.
The speaker says, "Last week, only three of our twelve members showed up to the afternoon meeting."
This gives a specific number that shows few members attend in the afternoon.
So the evidence is that only three of twelve members came to the afternoon meeting last week.
